obs_1: **Spending outpaces returns** : The 69% withdrawal rate runs 13.8 times higher than the portfolio's expected return, so in an average year the savings would shrink in real terms rather than grow. This tension would ease most if the spending target or the savings base shifted before retirement begins.
obs_2: **Half the gap stays yours** : Government income covers 43% of your $3,800 monthly spending, which leaves the larger share resting on a savings layer that is still forming. The plan's fragility traces back to this split far more than to the size of the benefits themselves.
obs_3: **The rate falls to zero** : Your effective tax moves from 15% now to 0% in retirement, a difference near $9,000 a year, because projected retirement income sits low enough to fall outside taxable territory. That zero rate is a signal the savings layer would be producing little income, not a sign of efficiency.
obs_4: **Time as the quiet lever** : With 33 years before retirement, each dollar set aside now has the longest possible runway to compound, which is why early changes weigh more than later ones. This is the one advantage a 32-year-old holds that no retiree can recover.
obs_5: **Where the accounts sit** : Your savings split into $18,000 in a Registered Retirement Savings Plan and $12,000 in a Tax-Free Savings Account, so more than half already carries future tax while the rest grows tax-free. This balance shapes how flexibly you could draw income later, beyond simply how much accumulates.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years closest to now carry the most weight, since the 33-year runway gives early contributions the longest time to compound. A change made at 32 would have more room to build than the same change made a decade later. The next update of this assessment, in 12 months, would measure how the plan responds to any adjustments you make in the meantime.
model_blind_spots: This model does not capture how your income or contributions might change across a 33-year career, which for someone early in their path could shift the outcome more than any market assumption. It also cannot foresee life events such as a career change, an inheritance, or a partnership, each of which would reshape the savings picture. These dimensions could be explored with the interactive Laboratoire.
